newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma HRW wheat crop seen at 109.9 mln bushels.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma HRW wheat crop seen at 109.9 mln bushels.

text.p: A group touring Oklahoma wheat fields projected the state's 1997 hard red winter wheat crop this year at 109.9 million bushels with a yield of 22 bushels an acre on five million acres, one of the tour's organizers said.

The tour was sponsored by Oklahoma grain and seed company Johnston Enterprises and had 150 participants, including representatives of the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Farm Service Agency and Oklahoma State University, private crop consultant Dale Fain said.

A survey conducted by Oklahoma State University in late April projected this year's crop at 121.34 million bushels, and noted that prior to the recent freeze, the state had the potential to produce 205.39 million.
USDA estimated the state's production in 1996 at 93.1 million bushels with a yield of 19 bushels an acre.
"It is getting worse every day. The freeze this year caused stem damage and the longer the plant stays in the field, the more freeze damage will become apparent," Fain said.
Fain, a former extension agronomist at Oklahoma State University, said the final production total for the state could be even lower than the tour's projection.

"I think as we get into typical maturing weather of May and early June these plants will just deteoriate and will be down lodged. There is no strength in the straw. I saw fields yesterday (Monday) which were already going down," he said.
Fain also anticipated the freeze damage to the Kansas crop could be worse than many currently believe.

"The Kansas crop is behind ours and still looks good. You drive down the road at sixty miles an hour you think you've got a lot of 50-bushel wheat but it is just not there," he said. "A lot of people projecting good yields are going to be disappointed. The freeze didn't stop at the Oklahoma border."

"I think you're going to see a lot of real pretty wheat fields. You're going to put the combine in and there won't be any wheat in the head. I think that is going to be the scenario we are going to live with this year," he added.
Fain said the tour found widespread leaf rust, tan spot and septoria throughout Oklahoma.
"Rust is a major problem throughout the state. It is everywhere," Fain said, noting that diseases could further deteriorate head size and test weights.
Fain noted, however, that most of this year's losses would be due to freeze rather than disease.
